> Physical evidence update 2026-11-07: read the complete [upgrade report](../PHYSICAL_UPGRADE_REPORT.md) and the new physical studies in `data/physical_studies.jsonl`. Earlier source accounts below retain their publication scopes.

> Version discrepancy: the later official team page specifies a 3.5-inch aluminum drum; the retained interview account below describes steel. Exact revision is unresolved. Do not silently combine them.

# 2026-1678: Protected carbon intake and continuous J-path launcher feed

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A 2×1 aluminum crash member protects a carbon intake roller. Later wrist plates use half-inch stock with raised hard-stop contact regions and pocketing. The shooter uses a J-shaped accelerating tunnel, a separate feeder, a four-X60 steel drum and powered hood rollers; its hood pivot is supported independently of the drum. Two side cameras were added to the original front Limelight.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The team links the crash member to allowing a light but impact-sensitive roller, larger hard-stop contact to reduced wear, low electronics/wiring to a lower floor, and additional cameras to midfield vision gaps found at Half Moon Bay. The source also describes replacing an earlier S-shaped path after direction reversal hurt consistency.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

The useful package combines structural load routing with flow continuity. The crash member must intercept contact before the carbon roller does; copying only the carbon tube removes the condition that made it practical. A lower floor reduces the climb imposed on loose fuel, while a J-path avoids reversing the velocity component that was just created upstream. Independent hood support can reduce parasitic coupling, but hood and drum still need controlled compression over their complete angle range. The camera change is evidence that good scoring performance near the hub did not guarantee adequate pose observability in midfield.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Measure path velocity and compression through hood travel, inspect crash loads with the collector extended, and compare localization availability in midfield before and after adding side views. Retain a separate shooter-ready gate before enabling the floor.

## Limits

Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

# 2026-1678: Limestone official page; interview discrepancies retained

Generated from `data/physical_studies.jsonl`; edit that authoritative record.

## Whole robot and packaging

A front collector and horizontally sliding wall feed a broad floor inside a square drivebase. The launcher stands across the rear; the floor hinges upward from its rear attachment to expose the electrical bay beneath. Intake-end floor supports rest on module-mounted hard stops and a retaining pin prevents unintended lifting. The hopper grows horizontally with the intake and vertically with a climber-linked upper enclosure. The whole render establishes the front-to-rear arrangement but does not establish every swept clearance. The battery and electronics are low, below the transport floor; the inspected electrical render shows component placement with the floor removed, not a complete battery-change sequence.

## Piece flow

Fuel enters the front rollers, passes over the collector pivot and onto a floor with tube rollers and flex-wheel rollers. The floor feeds a curved tunnel, which turns travel upward toward the drum. Feeder, accelerating backing contacts, drum and hood share responsibility for the final entry state. The earlier interview calls the later path J-shaped and reports abandoning an S path; the new page is a separate publication snapshot. It names a different drum material from the retained interview, so do not fuse both descriptions into one certified build.

## Annotated views

Editorial reconstruction. Not to scale; only explicit dimension labels are source dimensions. No CAD-derived measurements. Dashed envelopes are schematic and not clearance certification.

## Protected roller and post-acquisition guides

### Published construction

The retained account describes a carbon roller behind an aluminum crash member. The inspected team CAD render shows the collector transmission, deployment hardware and slotted hopper side plates.

### Team rationale / attribution boundary

Read cited historical note for team rationale; the operating reconstruction below is editorial and does not establish additional team intent.

### Editorial operating reconstruction

The main powered contact lifts fuel inward; downstream guides must stop it from touching the pickup roller again. Opening the collector also moves the hopper wall, so successful deployment is a prerequisite for the intended acquisition volume.

### Engineering interpretation

A crash member needs to intercept the expected collision before a fragile roller does. Its position relative to the ground mouth is therefore as important as its section. A guard that is too low could push fuel away; a guard too far behind the roller could fail to protect it.

### Transfer and compatibility limits

Transfer the protection and supported bumper crossing together. Do not copy lightweight roller construction without the protective load path.

### Unknowns

Exact crash deflection, ground clearance, compression and stage-specific source chronology remain unresolved.

### Proposed validation, not performed

First inspect the missing source interface or CAD; only then test the specific capture/transfer failure that could change the architecture. No hardware experiment was performed in this upgrade.

## Hinged mixed-contact floor and service access

### Published construction

The official page specifies five 1-inch tube rollers and three 2-inch flex-wheel rollers. It gives floor reductions of 1.5:1 and 3:1 respectively and describes pivot-up electrical access.

### Team rationale / attribution boundary

The floor receives fuel at the intake edge, advances it through the steeper wheel region, and supplies the rear tunnel. For maintenance, release the retainer and pivot the floor upward rather than dismantling the launcher.

### Engineering interpretation

Different shaft speeds can yield the same nominal surface speed when diameter doubles. That is a useful check, not a measured ball-speed result: under the usual reduction convention, 1/1.5 equals 2/3. Slip, grip and compression can still differ. This arrangement also keeps electrical service space out of the operating inventory path.

## J-path feed, drum and independently supported hood

### Published construction

The interview describes a separate feeder and independently supported hood pivot. The official page specifies a 3.5-inch aluminum drum and a 25-inch spacing between shooter side plates; it describes a 2-inch feeder and 1.25-inch backing contacts.

### Team rationale / attribution boundary

Read cited historical note for team rationale; the operating reconstruction below is editorial and does not establish additional team intent.

### Editorial operating reconstruction

Floor delivery enters the rising curve; successive powered surfaces accelerate it before the drum/hood release. Hood adjustment changes launch geometry while feed remains aligned with the entry.

### Engineering interpretation

A gradual turn can avoid undoing upstream velocity, but only if piece support and compression persist around the curve. Independent hood support keeps hood loads from depending entirely on drum bearings; it does not make drum-to-hood clearance constant automatically.

### Transfer and compatibility limits

Transfer continuous supported acceleration and independent hood structure. The new hood range, power and stiffness must preserve the same feed constraint; no turret is required for those features.

### Unknowns

Material conflict: retained interview says steel; official page says aluminum. Exact revision, compression over hood travel and live electrical budget are unresolved.

### Proposed validation, not performed

First inspect the missing source interface or CAD; only then test the specific capture/transfer failure that could change the architecture. No hardware experiment was performed in this upgrade.

## Horizontal storage tied to intake, vertical storage tied to climb

### Published construction

The official page describes slotted sliding side panels and a separate vertical extension tied to the climber. Inspected renders show both panel overlap and tall rear structure.

### Team rationale / attribution boundary

Read cited historical note for team rationale; the operating reconstruction below is editorial and does not establish additional team intent.

### Editorial operating reconstruction

Collector deployment draws the lower wall outward; the upper enclosure changes height through the separate lift. Containment must remain continuous where those motions meet.

### Engineering interpretation

These are two degrees of storage change, not one generic expanding hopper. A substitute fixed roof may remove vertical motion but also reduce volume and change retention. Low-fill evacuation depends on where the floor remains exposed after retraction.

### Transfer and compatibility limits

Horizontal storage can transfer independently only after separating the vertical enclosure support. A climber-linked roof cannot be removed without redesigning its support and retention.

### Unknowns

physical_studies.piece_flow: Fuel enters the front rollers, passes over the collector pivot and onto a floor with tube rollers and flex-wheel rollers. The floor feeds a curved tunnel, which turns travel upward toward the drum. Feeder, accelerating backing contacts, drum and hood share responsibility for the final entry state. It names a different drum material from the retained interview, so do not fuse both descriptions into one certified build.

source_reviews.review_basis: Read original team replies via Discourse JSON

source_review.whole_robot_explanation: Limestone packages a full-width intake, a floor with changing roller geometry and a staged launch tunnel on a compact swerve base. Citrus Circuits’ season page is unusually useful for distinguishing what each contact is intended to do. The intake guides newly acquired fuel away from the main roller, the floor addresses bridging near the feeder, and the tunnel supplies a substantial share of the launch speed before final acceleration. Hopper expansion and Level 1 climbing share structure, so usable volume, clearance and endgame geometry cannot be analyzed independently.
piece_flow: The slapdown intake uses a silicone-covered main roller, a kicker and smaller guide contacts to keep fuel from returning to the first roller.
Five dead-axle rollers and three flex-wheel rollers form the floor. A steeper compliant section is intended to reduce wedging as fuel approaches the feeder.

Powered backing contacts constrain fuel through the rising tunnel. The team page describes approximately 70 percent of shot speed before final acceleration by the drum and mechanically linked hood rollers.
source_review.packaging_and_motion: The team lists a 27-inch-square MK5n chassis. The floor pivots for access to battery and electronics, rests on hard stops in operation and is retained by a pin. Horizontal hopper extension is linked to the collector through a slotted connection. The team also describes vertical extension associated with the climb assembly. Check both motions with a packed hopper and a deflected wall, particularly where a shared mechanism must return to a clearance-critical pose.

subsystems.name: Collector and expanding storage
subsystems.construction: Full-width pivoting collector, silicone-covered carbon main roller, crash bar and replaceable SRPP plates. Slotted horizontal connection and vertical climb-linked extension.
subsystems.operation: Sweep in fuel and retain it while linked structures move.
subsystems.team_rationale: Official description links guide contacts to preventing recontact and impact parts to rapid replacement.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Keep crash structure above the effective fuel approach while protecting the roller under angled impacts.
subsystems.interfaces: The intake sweep drives hopper geometry and must clear the floor stops.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Check replaceable plate and slot wear as well as the effort to restore alignment after a strike.
subsystems.unknowns: Impact load and loaded route retention.

subsystems.name: Floor, tunnel and launch
subsystems.construction: Sloped roller floor, active backing and separate powered feed roller. Official page lists aluminum drum and linked driven hood rollers.
subsystems.operation: Present and accelerate fuel in successive contacts. Pivot the floor for service after releasing its retaining pin.
subsystems.team_rationale: The team intended the sloped compliant contacts to reduce keystoning and the tunnel to deliver a controlled entry speed.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: The roller path should maintain capture at the last low-speed to high-speed boundary. Verify release uniformity across the width.
subsystems.interfaces: Floor latch, first tunnel contact and backing rollers must agree under deflection.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Check sleeve migration at speed where used and service-floor return alignment.
subsystems.unknowns: Actual drum revision and controlled lane-by-lane data.

revisions: Reveal discussion describes silicone expansion at high shooter speed, while the later team page describes a grip-tape-covered 3.5-inch aluminum drum.
The older interview synopsis described steel. Exact association among the interview, reveal thread and final team specifications remains unverified.
The team page documents a hot-swappable impact protection approach and integrated horizontal and vertical hopper expansion.
transferable_principles: Design the collector exit so captured fuel cannot reenter the first powered nip.
Use floor geometry and compliant contacts to change how pieces load one another at a narrow transition.
Verify service-floor retention as a performance requirement, since its operating position defines the feed boundary.
disconfirming_conditions: More preacceleration can create bounce or slug feeding if the drum cannot accept the presented stream.
A shared climb and hopper structure can lose value if wear or impact couples a storage problem into both operating modes.
A change in drum material or surface can invalidate release calibration and loaded recovery comparisons.
remaining_gaps: Exact event mapping for drum construction, launch-rate and energy recovery traces, and complete validation of loaded motion and clearance.
recommended_images: Official Limestone side and isolated drivetrain views for the floor pivot and latch. Request a cutaway of the rising tunnel and deployed hopper linkage.
